label: q1-data
topic: Q1 enhancer-promoter specificity: public data and a first analysis (GSE186265, Martinez-Ara et al. 2022, mouse ES cells)
summary: Dataset: GEO GSE186265 (Martinez-Ara, van Steensel lab, Mol Cell 2022): combinatorial reporter assay of DHS-centred candidate CREs ('enhancers') x promoters from three mouse loci, 3 biological replicates, upstream placement. After pooling orientations/locus libraries to one value per replicate per (enhancer, promoter) cell, 232 enhancers x 31 promoters, 3747 cells (52% filled). Analysed the largest complete block found by a deterministic greedy rule: 98 enhancers x 15 promoters (105 promoter pairs). log2(activity+0.01). Noise = pooled replicate SD in deciles of cell mean (about 1.0 log2 for the weakest 40% of cells, 0.16-0.20 for the strongest 30%). Results (point estimate, bootstrap 95% interval where stated): (1) rank agreement between promoters is weak and variable: Spearman median 0.38 (range -0.29 to 0.72 over the 105 pairs), Kendall tau-b median 0.27 (range -0.19 to 0.52). A purely multiplicative model with the same replicate noise predicts Spearman median 0.81, so all 105 pairs fall below the null's 95% lower bound; per-promoter replicate reliability is high (median 0.96, min 0.72), so this is not replicate noise. (2) Among enhancer pairs whose order is significant (|z|>2) on both promoters of a promoter pair, a median 26.5% (range 9.6-63.5%) are in opposite order; summed over the 105 pairs 65,174 of 224,658 doubly-significant comparisons reverse, against 368 (95% 196-624) expected from noise under a multiplicative model; at |z|>3, 43,854 vs 4.4. The mean size of a reversal (min of the two absolute log2 differences) has median 1.33 log2 over pairs (max 2.52). The most extreme pair, P007 vs P021, has Spearman -0.29 (enhancer+replicate bootstrap -0.47 to -0.10). (3) Spectrum: on the linear matrix the best rank-one fit explains 71.3% of the sum of squares (rep-bootstrap 70.8-71.6%, enhancer+rep 67.2-76.2%); on the log2 matrix 75.7% (uncentered) and 61.6% (grand-mean centred). Because a multiplicative model is rank one on the LINEAR scale and ADDITIVE (row+column effects, not rank one) on the log scale, the more telling log-scale split is: additive row+column effects 73.3% of variance, interaction 26.7% (enh+rep 23.8-30.1%), interaction 11.9x the size expected from replicate noise alone (10.7-13.4), 25.0% after subtracting noise; the best rank-one fit of that interaction captures 38.5% of it (31.7-44.6%); additive + rank-one interaction = 83.6%. Conclusion: in this dataset multiplicativity is a good first approximation for about three quarters of the variance but is rejected as an exact model; the order of enhancer strengths changes materially between promoters (promoter-specific interaction), beyond measurement noise, and the interaction has more than one dimension. Caveats: cCREs are DHS fragments not validated enhancers; promoter-pair correlations are strongly structured (clusters such as P013/P014/P021 correlate ~0.7); orientations and locus libraries pooled; one dataset, one cell type; this is mouse ES cells not human.
lay_summary: Imagine 98 loudspeakers (enhancers) each wired to 15 different light bulbs (promoters), and we record how bright each bulb gets. If every speaker simply multiplied every bulb's brightness by a fixed amount, the speakers would rank the same way for every bulb. We found they do not: for typical pairs of bulbs, the speakers' ranking agrees only weakly, and in about a quarter of the clear-cut comparisons the order is flipped. Simple multiplication still explains roughly three quarters of the variation, but the rest is a real bulb-specific effect, about twelve times larger than measurement noise. So an enhancer is not just 'strong' or 'weak'; how strong it looks depends on which promoter it is paired with.

findings.claim: GSE186265 contains reporter-assay activities for many enhancer(cCRE) x promoter pairs from three mouse loci with 3 biological replicates; a usable supplementary file is GSE186265_Activities_allcombinations_Upstream.tsv.gz (5,837,300 bytes).
findings.evidence_quote: 3 Biological replicates of cDNA samples for each library mix, 2 pDNA replicates for each library mix and 1 iPCR sequencing run per separate library.

findings.claim: The upstream file has 10,678 EP rows covering 232 distinct enhancer fragments x 31 distinct promoter fragments; pooling orientations/locus libraries gives 3747 filled cells of 7192 (52%).
findings.source: own calculation: scripts/q1-data/01_blocks.py and 02_build_matrix.py on the downloaded file

findings.claim: Largest complete block (greedy, deterministic) is 98 enhancers x 15 promoters, giving 105 promoter pairs.
Spearman correlation between promoters over the 98 shared enhancers: median 0.382, range -0.286 to 0.715 across 105 pairs (log2(activity+0.01)).
Kendall tau-b between promoters: median 0.269, range -0.190 to 0.522.

Bootstrap intervals for the extreme pairs: P014 vs P021 Spearman 0.715 (replicate bootstrap 0.675-0.746; enhancer+replicate 0.563-0.808); P007 vs P021 Spearman -0.286 (replicate bootstrap -0.317 to -0.259; enhancer+replicate -0.471 to -0.095). Interval for every pair is in panel_pairs_main.json (B=1000).

Replicate noise alone cannot explain the weak agreement: under a purely multiplicative (log-additive) model with the estimated replicate noise, the median pair Spearman would be 0.812; all 105 observed pair Spearmans lie below the null 95% lower bound. Per-promoter replicate reliability median 0.962, min 0.722 (P015).
findings.source: own calculation: summary_main.json (null_rho_median_of_pairs, promoter_reliability_spearman); 500 null simulations

findings.claim: Rank reversals (|z|>2 on both promoters, opposite sign): 65,174 of 224,658 doubly-significant enhancer-pair comparisons summed over 105 promoter pairs (29.0%; per-pair median fraction 26.5%, range 9.6-63.5%). Null expectation under multiplicative model + noise: 368 (95% 196-624). At |z|>3: 43,854 observed vs 4.4 expected.

Typical reversal magnitude: mean over reversed enhancer pairs of min(|log2 difference on promoter a|, |on promoter b|) has median 1.33 log2 across promoter pairs (max 2.52, i.e. about 5.7-fold at both promoters).

Best rank-one fit explains 71.3% of the sum of squares of the linear-scale 98x15 matrix (replicate bootstrap 70.8-71.6%; enhancer+replicate bootstrap 67.2-76.2%). Linear singular values: 79.9, 37.8, 20.9, 19.2, 11.1, 8.5, 6.9, 6.5, 5.2, 2.8, 2.3, 2.2, 1.9, 1.7, 1.4.

On log2 scale: best rank-one fit explains 75.7% (uncentered) / 61.6% (grand-mean centred) of the sum of squares; additive row+column effects explain 73.3% of variance about the grand mean, the row x column interaction 26.7% (enh+rep CI 23.8-30.1%). Uncentered log singular values: 91.3, 28.6, 26.5, 15.6, 13.0, ... 4.1.

Interaction sum of squares is 11.9x the amount expected from replicate noise alone (replicate bootstrap 12.0-12.4; enhancer+replicate 10.7-13.4); 25.0% of variance after subtracting the noise expectation. Best rank-one fit of the interaction explains 38.5% of it (31.7-44.6%); additive plus rank-one interaction explains 83.6%.
findings.source: own calculation: summary_main.json (svd.interaction_ss_over_noise etc.). Noise expectation = mean SE^2 x (nE-1)(nP-1) assumes homoscedastic-like errors; approximate.

findings.claim: Results are robust to the pseudocount and threshold: pseudocount 0.03 gives Spearman median 0.378, reversal fraction 0.265, interaction/noise 17.3; pseudocount 0.003 gives 0.378, 0.263, 8.8; z=3 gives reversal fraction 0.222. Linear rank-one share 0.713 in all.
Restricting to the more active enhancers does not restore agreement: top 50% by mean activity (n=49) Spearman median 0.355; top 25% (n=25) 0.385.

All 363 promoter pairs with at least 20 shared enhancers (pairwise-complete, all 31 promoters): Spearman median 0.312 (range -0.574 to 0.838), median reversal fraction 0.252. Per-pair table in allpairs_main.csv (point estimates only, no bootstrap).
The original authors report that more than half of the tested CREs show significant promoter selectivity (independent support for promoter-specific enhancer effects).
findings.evidence_quote: By systematic reporter assays of thousands of CRE – promoter pairs from three Mb-sized genomic regions in mouse cells, we found that CREs vary substantially in their promoter compatibility, with more than half showing significant selectivity.

findings.claim: Martinez-Ara et al. note that Bergman et al. (human K562) proposed multiplicative combination of enhancer and promoter activity while both datasets also show selectivity.
findings.evidence_quote: Based on mathematical modeling of their data, the authors proposed that intrinsic cCRE and P activities generally combine multiplicatively to determine reporter activity.

findings.claim: Design: three 1-3 Mb loci, a large fraction of all pairwise cCRE-promoter combinations, each element in two orientations.
findings.evidence_quote: From these loci, which each encompass ∼20 genes, we tested a large fraction of all possible pairwise cCRE-promoter (cCRE-P) combinations.

key_claims.claim: The data have the same 98 enhancers (DHS-centred cCREs) measured on 15 promoters with 3 replicates, in a public GEO file.
key_claims.evidence_quote: 3 Biological replicates of cDNA samples for each library mix, 2 pDNA replicates for each library mix and 1 iPCR sequencing run per separate library.

key_claims.claim: Promoter-to-promoter rank agreement is weak (Spearman median 0.38, range -0.29 to 0.72) and well below the 0.81 expected for a purely multiplicative model with the same noise.
About 26% of doubly-significant enhancer-pair orderings reverse between promoters (65,174 of 224,658 overall), versus 368 expected from noise.
Best rank-one (multiplicative) fit explains 71% of the linear-scale matrix; the log-scale interaction is 27% of variance and 11.9x noise, so multiplicativity is a good approximation but not exact.

recommendations: Treat the multiplicative (rank-one in linear scale) model as the baseline to be refuted: here it fits ~71% but fails against the noise null, so Lean statements about rank-one classes can be tested with this 98x15 matrix (scratch/q1-data/matrix.npz, panel lists in summary_main.json).

Repeat on a second public dataset (e.g. Bergman et al. 2022 human K562 ExP STARR-seq) to see whether the 27% interaction share and ~26% reversal fraction replicate; I did not locate or download its processed table.
Next analysis: orientation-resolved matrices and a held-out-promoter prediction test of rank-one vs rank-two models.

could_not_find: Bergman et al. 2022 processed data table: the paper is not open access in Europe PMC and I did not locate its accession, so the K562 ExP data were not analysed.
Zenodo 6406791 (EPCombinations code, 86.8 MB) was not downloaded; GEO supplementary files were sufficient.
The 'enhancers' are DHS-centred candidate cis-regulatory elements, not individually validated enhancers; no independent enhancer validation was checked.

Replicate noise is estimated from only 3 replicates per cell via pooled decile variances, and the bootstrap resamples replicates per cell independently (ignores shared batch effects); intervals for rank statistics from the replicate bootstrap are therefore narrow and the enhancer+replicate bootstrap is the more honest interval.

The point estimate of interaction share (0.267) lies just below its replicate-bootstrap interval (0.269-0.277) because resampling replicates adds noise; the bootstrap is a spread measure here, not bias-corrected.
Orientation and locus-library effects were pooled by averaging and not analysed separately; the panel was chosen by a greedy rule, not an optimal complete block.
